JOINT BANK ACCOUNTS AND SURVIVORSHIP RIGHTS — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · Jordan Alex Lee

DECLARATION
This information sheet describes Jordan Alex Lee and Morgan Lee's joint account at First California Bank under California's Multiple-Party Accounts Law (California Probate Code Part 2 of Division 5, commencing with § 5100). It states what California law provides about ownership and survivorship of a joint account; it is not a signature card, account agreement, or other paperwork that itself opens, modifies, or closes any account.

WHAT A JOINT ACCOUNT IS
"California's Multiple-Party Accounts Law" is the statute's own short title, given at Probate Code § 5100, for Part 2 of Division 5 of the Probate Code (§§ 5100-5407). Within that law, § 5130 defines a "joint account" as an account payable on request to one or more of two or more parties, whether or not the account mentions any right of survivorship — meaning the label "joint account" does not by itself say who gets the funds if one owner dies; that question is answered by separate provisions of the same law, addressed below. A joint account is one of three statutorily defined account types under this law. The other two — a P.O.D. (payable-on-death) account and a Totten trust account — are addressed in this corpus's separate Payable-on-Death (POD) Account Designation information sheet, which this document does not duplicate.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-09]
  "This part may be cited as the California Multiple-Party Accounts Law."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 5100, California Probate Code, short title of the Multiple-Party Accounts Law (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=5100.)
  "“Joint account” means an account payable on request to one or more of two or more parties whether or not mention is made of any right of survivorship."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 5130, California Probate Code, definition of "joint account" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=5130.)
  Known gap: The "multiple-party account" umbrella definition (which lists a joint account as one of three types alongside a P.O.D. account and a Totten trust account) is quoted in this corpus's Payable-on-Death (POD) Account Designation information sheet rather than repeated here, to avoid a duplicate citation of identical statutory text. The § 5100 and § 5130 citations quoted directly below were independently fetched for this document from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov and were not previously quoted elsewhere in this corpus.

OWNERSHIP BETWEEN THE PARTIES DURING THEIR LIFETIMES
While all parties to a joint account are alive, § 5301 governs who owns the funds on deposit as between them — a different question from who receives the funds if a party dies, addressed separately below. By default, an account belongs to the parties in proportion to each party's net contributions, unless clear and convincing evidence shows a different intent. If a party withdraws more than that party's own net contribution — an "excess withdrawal" — the other parties gain an ownership interest in the excess, in proportion to their own net contributions to what remained on deposit immediately afterward, unless clear and convincing evidence shows a contrary agreement between the parties. Only a living party — or a conservator, guardian, or agent acting on that living party's behalf — may bring a claim to recover that ownership interest in an excess withdrawal; the statute gives a court discretion to reduce any such recovery, in the interest of justice, to reflect funds already withdrawn and applied for the claiming party's benefit.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-09]
  "An account belongs, during the lifetime of all parties, to the parties in proportion to the net contributions by each, unless there is clear and convincing evidence of a different intent."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 5301(a), California Probate Code, joint account ownership during the parties' lifetimes (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=5301.)
  "If a party makes an excess withdrawal from an account, the other parties to the account shall have an ownership interest in the excess withdrawal in proportion to the net contributions of each to the amount on deposit in the account immediately following the excess withdrawal, unless there is clear and convincing evidence of a contrary agreement between the parties."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 5301(b), California Probate Code, ownership interest arising from an excess withdrawal (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=5301.)
  "Only a living party, or a conservator, guardian, or agent acting on behalf of a living party, shall be permitted to make a claim to recover the living party’s ownership interest in an excess withdrawal, pursuant to subdivision (b)."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 5301(c), California Probate Code, who may claim recovery of an excess withdrawal (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=5301.)
  Known gap: This is the lifetime ownership rule alone; it does not describe what happens to a joint account's funds when a party dies, which is a separate rule addressed in the next section. Subdivisions (d) and (e) of the same § 5301, which state that a P.O.D. payee or Totten trust beneficiary has no lifetime rights to an account's funds, describe different account types than a joint account and are outside this document's scope; they are addressed, alongside the definitions of those account types, in this corpus's Payable-on-Death (POD) Account Designation information sheet. Subdivision (f)'s definition of "excess withdrawal" is paraphrased above rather than separately quoted.

SURVIVORSHIP AT A PARTY'S DEATH
When a party to a joint account dies, § 5302(a) provides that the sums remaining on deposit belong to the surviving party or parties, as against the decedent's estate, unless clear and convincing evidence shows a different intent — the rule that lets a joint account pass to a surviving co-owner without going through probate. If two or more parties survive, their ownership shares afterward are in proportion to their previous § 5301 net-contribution ownership shares, augmented by an equal share of whatever interest the decedent owned in the account immediately before death; and the right of survivorship continues to apply between the remaining surviving parties for any later death among them.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-09]
  "Sums remaining on deposit at the death of a party to a joint account belong to the surviving party or parties as against the estate of the decedent unless there is clear and convincing evidence of a different intent. If there are two or more surviving parties, their respective ownerships during lifetime are in proportion to their previous ownership interests under Section 5301 augmented by an equal share for each survivor of any interest the decedent may have owned in the account immediately before the decedent’s death; and the right of survivorship continues between the surviving parties."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 5302(a), California Probate Code, survivorship of a joint account at a party's death (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=5302.)
  Known gap: § 5302(a) opens "Subject to Section 5040" — a cross-reference to a separate statutory section this document did not independently fetch or verify, and its text is not restated here. Subdivisions (b) through (e) of § 5302, which apply the survivorship rule specifically to P.O.D. accounts and Totten trust accounts rather than joint accounts, and which state that a right of survivorship cannot be changed by will, are outside this document's scope and are not quoted here, to avoid duplicating this corpus's existing Payable-on-Death (POD) Account Designation information sheet, which addresses them directly.

THE ACCOUNT'S FORM CONTROLS, AND HOW IT CAN BE CHANGED
§ 5303(a) makes the form of the account at the time of a party's death the controlling fact for the survivorship rule described above — the way the account was actually opened and left standing, not any later, separate expression of intent, is what determines whether a surviving party takes the balance. During a party's lifetime, § 5303(c) allows the terms of the account to be changed, by the methods described elsewhere in the same section, to eliminate or add a right of survivorship.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-09]
  "The provisions of Section 5302 as to rights of survivorship are determined by the form of the account at the death of a party."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 5303(a), California Probate Code, the account's form at death determines survivorship (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=5303.)
  "During the lifetime of a party, the terms of the account may be changed as provided in subdivision (b) to eliminate or to add rights of survivorship."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 5303(c), California Probate Code, changing survivorship rights during a party's lifetime (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=5303.)
  Known gap: § 5303(b)'s own list of methods for changing a multiple-party account's terms — closing and reopening the account, presenting a signed modification agreement, following a method the account's own terms provide, or the method described in § 5405(c) — and § 5303(c)'s further statement that withdrawing funds also reduces survivorship rights to the extent of the withdrawal, are both already quoted in this corpus's Payable-on-Death (POD) Account Designation information sheet and are not repeated here; that document's description of those methods applies to a joint account exactly as it does to a P.O.D. account, since § 5303 governs "multiple-party accounts" generally, not any one account type.

A JOINT ACCOUNT'S SURVIVORSHIP RIGHT IS VALID WITHOUT WILL FORMALITIES
§ 5304 states that a surviving joint account party's statutory right to the sums on deposit is not denied, abridged, or affected by the fact that the right was not created through a writing that meets the state's usual requirements for a valid testamentary disposition of property — a joint account's survivorship right is not treated as an attempted will, and does not have to comply with a will's execution formalities to be effective.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-09]
  "The right under this part of a surviving party to a joint account, or of a beneficiary, or of a P.O.D. payee, to the sums on deposit on the death of a party to a multiple-party account shall not be denied, abridged, or affected because such right has not been created by a writing executed in accordance with the laws of this state prescribing the requirements to effect a valid testamentary disposition of property."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 5304, California Probate Code, a joint account survivor's right is not testamentary (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=5304.)
  Known gap: § 5304's first sentence, which independently states that transfers under § 5302 are effective by reason of the account contract and this part and are not to be considered testamentary, is already quoted in this corpus's Payable-on-Death (POD) Account Designation information sheet; the second sentence quoted here, which addresses a joint account survivor's right by name, was not previously quoted there and was independently fetched and verified for this document.

COMMUNITY PROPERTY FUNDS IN A JOINT ACCOUNT
Placing funds in a joint account between spouses does not, on its own, change whether those funds are community or separate property. § 5305(d) states that — apart from the burden-of-proof and anti-revocation-by-will rules addressed in the same section's other subdivisions — a multiple-party account created with community property funds does not in any way alter community property rights.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-09]
  "Except as provided in subdivisions (b) and (c), a multiple-party account created with community property funds does not in any way alter community property rights."
  — Cal. Prob. Code § 5305(d), California Probate Code, community property character of joint account funds is otherwise unchanged (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PROB&sectionNum=5305.)
  Known gap: § 5305(a)'s rebuttable presumption that a married couple's net contribution to an account is community property, and its rebuttal methods in subdivision (b), are already quoted and discussed in this corpus's Payable-on-Death (POD) Account Designation information sheet (which draws on the identical § 5305) and are not repeated here. § 5305(c)'s cross-reference to § 5307 (revocation of a right of survivorship on divorce) was not independently reverified for this document; that topic is likewise addressed in the POD information sheet via its own separately verified § 5307 citation.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT
This information sheet is a planning reference only. It does not open, modify, or close Jordan Alex Lee and Morgan Lee's account at First California Bank, does not itself create or remove a right of survivorship, and does not resolve any dispute between account parties or with a decedent's estate.

Prepared by Jordan Alex Lee on September 9, 2026, at Sacramento, California.

_________________________ Jordan Alex Lee   Date: September 9, 2026
